extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; economists and general readers interested in price theory and wages
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation of Adam Smith's classical principles on how market price relates to natural price, causes of deviations, and the determinants of wages of labour in a society with private property and accumulated stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market price determined by effectual demand vs quantity supplied
rubrics_metrics.description: When the quantity of any commodity brought to market falls short of the effectual demand, competition among those willing to pay more will raise the market price above the natural price; when quantity exceeds effectual demand, some part must be sold to buyers willing to pay less, and the market price will sink below the natural price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains directional relationship between supply relative to demand and market price. Examples: exorbitant prices during blockades or famine (short supply); import excess of perishable goods (large price falls). The degree of deviation depends on size of deficiency/excess and the eagerness/wealth of competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural price as central tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural price is the 'central price' toward which market prices continually gravitate; various accidents may keep market prices above or below it for periods, but they are constantly tending towards it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural price is defined by the cost components (rent, wages, profit) at their natural rates. Market price fluctuates around this centre due to transient causes; long-term forces (entry/exit of resources) push prices back toward the natural price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity brought to market adjusts to effectual demand via incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the interest of those who employ land, labour, or stock to bring to market a quantity neither exceeding nor falling short of the effectual demand; if supply exceeds demand some inputs withdraw, if supply falls short other inputs are attracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjustment mechanisms: landlords withdraw land, labourers withdraw labour, employers withdraw stock when supply > demand; conversely, landlords prepare more land and employers employ more labour/stock when supply < demand. These adjustments restore prices to natural rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability of produce by employment causes differing price volatility
rubrics_metrics.description: In some employments (e.g., husbandry) the same quantity of industry produces very different quantities in different years, causing larger fluctuations in market price; in others (e.g., spinning/weaving) equal industry produces nearly the same annually, leading to prices nearer their natural price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predicts that agricultural commodities exhibit greater price volatility than manufactured goods because supply is less predictable. Example: linen and woollen cloth prices vary mainly with demand; corn prices vary with both demand and large supply fluctuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-term fluctuations mainly affect wages and profit, not rent
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional and temporary fluctuations in the market price of a commodity fall chiefly upon those parts of its price which resolve themselves into wages and profit; rent, especially a rent certain in money, is much less affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money rents fixed by lease are stable; share rents’ yearly value changes with produce price but rate seldom changes because landlords and tenants set leases based on average prices, not temporary fluctuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrets and monopolies can keep market price above natural price
rubrics_metrics.description: If suppliers conceal increased effectual demand (or possess a secret or monopoly), they can keep the market understocked and sell above the natural price; secrets in manufactures and monopolies have similar effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secrets in trade may be temporary (difficult to keep); manufacturing secrets (e.g., cheaper dyeing method) can be kept longer. Monopolies and exclusive privileges maintain higher prices by restricting supply; their effects last as long as the restrictive policy or secrecy endures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly vs free competition price distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The price of monopoly is the highest which can be got (what buyers will consent to give); the natural price (price of free competition) is the lowest which sellers can commonly afford to take for any considerable time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames monopoly price as buyer-extracting and natural price as seller-sustaining. Use to evaluate policy effects: monopoly/privilege increases prices and emoluments above natural rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations that restrict competition act as enlarged monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive privileges of corporations, statutes of apprenticeship, and laws that restrain competition to fewer people than otherwise will tend to keep market price of particular commodities above the natural price and maintain higher wages/profits in those employments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such regulatory restrictions can have long-lasting effects on prices and incomes in affected employments; their duration matches the policy enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market price seldom stays below natural price in free competition
rubrics_metrics.description: When any part of the price is paid below its natural rate, those affected withdraw resources until supply reduces and market price rises to the natural price, provided there is perfect liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the asymmetry: falling below natural rates triggers withdrawal of supply, whereas staying above can be sustained by policy or natural scarcity. Regulatory constraints can make below-natural rates persist only under extreme, long-term restriction (e.g., enforced hereditary occupations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural price varies with natural rates of wages, profit, and rent
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural price itself varies with the natural rate of each of its component parts—wages, profit, and rent—and these rates vary according to the circumstances of society (riches or poverty, advancing, stationary, or declining).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals that to understand changes in natural prices one must analyze determinants of wages, profits, and rent in a society; subsequent chapters address wages, profit, proportion between them, and rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce of labour as the natural recompense (wages)
rubrics_metrics.description: The produce of labour constitutes the natural recompense or wages of labour; in the original state before appropriation of land and accumulation of stock, the whole produce of labour belonged to the labourer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical framing: after private property and capital accumulation, wages are reduced by rent and profit claims; this explains how wages are defined as the worker's share of product after deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rent and profit deductions reduce the labourer’s share
rubrics_metrics.description: As land becomes private property the landlord demands a share (rent) and masters advance maintenance/materials and claim profit, making deductions from the produce of labour; in many employments this separates wages from profits of stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the origins of distinct incomes (wages vs profits). Independent workmen who own stock both enjoy wages and profits; most workers work for masters who advance capital and thus claim profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages depend on contract and relative bargaining power of masters vs workmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Common wages depend on the usual contract between masters and workmen; masters, being fewer, can combine more easily (often tacitly) to keep wages down, while workmen’s combinations are often prohibited and less effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses institutional/legal context: laws permit masters' combinations and prohibit workmen’s; masters can sustain longer withholding because of accumulated stock; workmen’s combinations are often desperate, noisy, and seldom successful, sometimes punished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a subsistence minimum constrains how low wages can fall
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a certain rate, consistent with common humanity, below which ordinary wages cannot be reduced for any considerable time because a man must always live by his work; wages must be sufficient to maintain him and enable family continuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith references demographic considerations (raising children) and Cantillon’s estimate; precise proportion not fixed but emphasizes biological and social minimum sustaining the labour force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages rise with increasing demand for labour driven by rising revenue and stock
rubrics_metrics.description: When demand for those who live by wages continually increases (i.e., when revenue and stock destined to pay wages increase), masters must bid against one another, raising wages; increase of national wealth (particularly its growth) increases demand for labour and wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between absolute wealth and growth: thriving/growing societies (e.g., North America in Smith’s example) have higher wages than richer but stationary societies (e.g., China). Examples and colonial wage figures are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationary wealth leads to low wages despite overall riches
rubrics_metrics.description: If a country’s wealth has been long stationary, wages need not be high because the number of labourers easily supplies employment and masters have no need to bid for labour; thus high absolute wealth does not guarantee high wages without growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses China as an example of great but stationary wealth with low wages; contrasts with rapidly growing colonies where wages are higher even if absolute wealth is lower.
